turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Tuesday, the seventeenth of November. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed for the fourth time in a week. [pause] Oil fell three point six seven per cent.
[curious] A wall with no mortar in it, a hundred and five thousand eight hundred kilometres of the stuff, and the hammers are out of stock.
And in Dhaka, a revolution against an inherited certificate has issued thirteen thousand nine hundred and sixty-eight certificates of its own.
[thoughtful] That last one is going to sit with me all day. Start with the strait.
Sunday, before dawn. Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it flew six drones into an American air-defence radar at Riffa Air Base, in Bahrain.
Second time in three days?
Second time in three days. Residents heard blasts around four in the morning, and again at half past six.
Why Bahrain specifically?
Because that is where the American navy keeps its Gulf headquarters.
And the same statement said the strait was shut.
Same statement. The strait — quote — remained closed.
[skeptical] Right. Let's do the counting, because I know where this goes.

The Guard says six drones. US Central Command says it shot down two, no casualties, no damage. Bahrain's own military says — several. Bahrain condemned what it called the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory. Tehran's spokesman called the strikes purely defensive, and cited the United Nations Charter.
[wry] Everybody's lawyer is awake.
Friday's raid was framed as revenge for an American strike at Sirik, which is on Iran's own coast.
Then the tankers. This is the bit I don't trust.

Nor should you, yet. The Guard said two tankers hit mines in the southern strait. A state news agency reported one of them, carrying over two million barrels, had sunk. On Monday Iran's navy claimed a fourth tanker alight inside twenty-four hours. Reuters noted that the statement did not identify the tanker, its flag, its cargo, or the status of its crew.
[exhales] So no name, no flag, no crew.

One hull is independently attested. The crude carrier Al Dhannah, reported to the British maritime authority on the fifteenth, struck in the steering-gear room, turned around and went back to Dubai. Damaged, and afloat. That is the whole verified list.
Meanwhile Washington is parking ships.

The carrier Theodore Roosevelt arrived at the weekend and stayed, alongside the George H. W. Bush and the George Washington. Three American carriers in one sea. The analysts read it as miscalculation, not design — a political scientist at Chattanooga says both sides may prefer to avoid a full-scale war, but the danger lies in miscalculation. A researcher in Doha puts it plainly: each side believes it holds the stronger hand.
[thoughtful] Both convinced they're the one holding the stronger hand.
Now the sceptic, and it is the strongest thing on the page.
Go on.
Central Command's standing position, from the twenty-eighth of October, is that every primary transit route has been cleared of sea mines, and remains so.
And the traffic?

The cargo trackers put October at about fourteen million barrels a day still moving. Four-fifths of the pre-war figure. And here is the cleanest evidence of all. Brent fell three point six seven per cent on Monday — the session after the Guard said the strait was shut.
[scoffs] The market was told the tap was off and priced the opposite.
The reason traders gave was a forecast glut in the year after next. Not a blockade.
Okay. Thursday is going to be loud.
Beijing confirmed on Monday that its president will host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, together, in Shenzhen.
All three, in one room?

First time the leaders of those three countries have ever met face to face. The Kremlin put it on the record first, on the fourteenth. The subject is nuclear arms control. The last treaty capping the American and Russian arsenals expired in February, so the two largest stockpiles are uncapped for the first time in fifty years. Mr Trump refused a one-year extension. He wants a replacement that includes China, which has never agreed to cap anything.
And the expectation management?
A senior American official told Reuters — we do not expect to get to any kind of agreement.
[amused] That's the organisers briefing down their own summit.

And there is a second room that day. On the sixteenth the full European team joined the American-brokered Ukraine talks for the first time — Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, with the Commission, the Council and the Atlantic alliance. Berlin convenes on the nineteenth. The same Thursday. Warheads in Shenzhen with Ukraine off the agenda; Ukraine's allies in Berlin without Moscow.
Money. And I'm told the money all moved one way.

Everything fell but the dollar. Shares, bonds, gold, bitcoin and oil — together. One force, not five stories. Futures closed Monday pricing a rise in American rates on the ninth of December as a certainty — the next band at ninety-seven and a half per cent.
So a hundred per cent chance of a rise.
A hundred per cent, with a small tail on a double-sized move.
Walk me through why that drags everything down at once.

When money is expected to cost more, every future dollar of profit is worth less today. So shares fall, the currency paying the higher rate firms, and anything paying you nothing must compete with a bond that does. And gold touched three thousand eight hundred and thirty dollars, its weakest since October last year — on a day of open warfare in the Gulf.
[gasps] Gold fell during a shooting war.

Gold is pricing real yields and the dollar, not fear. The Nasdaq fell two point four nine per cent, a third straight loss. And global shares and global bonds fell together — the hedge moving the same way as the thing it is meant to hedge.
That's the part that should worry people.
It is explanation, not advice. But yes.
And the sceptic says the tail is wrong.

Futures put a half-point December move at two and a half per cent. Governor Christopher Waller has said that if October inflation ran hot, a fifty-basis-point rise should be considered — and that hiking only twenty-five would put the Federal Reserve's credibility at risk.
[deadpan] A sitting governor calling a quarter-point a credibility risk is not a two-and-a-half-per-cent event.
That is almost word for word what the desk wrote.
Singapore. And this one is ours.
On Monday the American Commerce Department's export-control bureau put Singapore on a five-country list for advanced computer chips. Indonesia, Malaysia, Brazil and Thailand are the others.
What does being on the list actually do?

You need a licence to ship chips here — and a licence to move them between buyers inside the country. Inside the country. The rule calls the five countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.
[pause] And how are the licences judged?
This is the sentence Singapore will be read on. Applications are weighed on the effectiveness of their export control regimes, and their coordination on the enforcement of export controls.
So our access to chips is now conditional on our own policing.

That is the whole of it. There is a hole in the middle of it, though: the requirement lifts where the end user is headquartered in the United States, which Fortune reads as exempting Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon.
[scoffs] So the biggest buyers walk through.
The teeth are in the second limb — a licence where an overseas data centre gives a Chinese or Macau firm more than twelve million units of processing power, under a stated presumption of denial.
When does the clock start?
It hasn't. The document still reads, in square brackets, insert date of publication in the Federal Register. Unfilled.
[chuckles] The rule naming us hasn't got a date on it.

Singapore answered the same day, jointly from the digital and trade ministries: they are studying the rule's details, and do not condone companies using their association with Singapore to circumvent the laws of other countries. No official named, no figure given, no deadline set.
And the case underneath it has moved on.
A fifth man was charged over diverted servers on the thirteenth. The Home Affairs Ministry had said four people and four companies on the twelfth. That was stale inside a day.
Nvidia reports tonight.
Tuesday afternoon in California, about twenty past one. Five twenty tomorrow morning here.
And still no chief executive.

Colette Kress is interim chief executive — a correction, by the way, we called her interim finance chief yesterday and that was wrong. Jensen Huang resigned on the twelfth, and the company has never said why.
What's the number to watch?

Not revenue. Obligation. At the end of July the balance sheet carried two hundred and seventy-nine billion dollars of long-term supply and capacity commitments. Three months earlier it was a hundred and nineteen.
[gasps] That more than doubled in a quarter.
Guidance is a hundred and eight billion dollars of revenue. Options imply an eight per cent move either way.
And Washington moved the day before.
It did. And the new rule's verdict on the rule it replaces is four words — never been enforced.
[laughs] They rescinded their own flagship control and wrote its obituary in the same document.
There's a footnote replacing artificial intelligence with super intelligence throughout, too.
Of course there is. Home lab — and keep it in English for me.

The free program most people use to run a chatbot on their own computer, rather than sending their words to a company's servers, reached version one on the thirteenth. Three and a half years after it was started.
Why does version one matter?

Because until now it moved fast enough that anything built on it could break week to week. Version one is a promise not to do that — where a tool stops being an experiment and becomes something a clinic or a law firm can build on.
And it got faster.

At the thing home machines are worst at. The best open systems are too big for the fast memory on a graphics card, so most of them sit in ordinary memory and get fetched piece by piece. The new build keeps what it has lately needed on the card and fetches the rest. On one high-end consumer card that took it from about thirty tokens a second to nearly sixty-eight. Roughly double. Although the patch this desk was watching is not the one that landed: a community submission from late August, sixty-seven comments deep, is still a draft awaiting two reviews that never came.
[sighs] And the one that shipped?
Opened in October by someone closer to the maintainers, merged in four days. One commenter put it bluntly — the expert-cache patches have not received significant review from code owners.
Kit. Apple.
Owners of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro are reporting eye strain, headaches and dizziness. On the sixteenth the measurement behind the complaint became public.
What's the mechanism?
To make grey, the panel switches its light on and off very fast and lets your eye average it out. Perfectly ordinary. Harmless when it is quick enough.
And here?
Measured at two hundred and forty hertz, at more than half of full depth, at every brightness below the very top.
Which compares to what?
The same laboratory measured last year's machine at fourteen thousand eight hundred and eighty hertz. Sixty times faster.
[exhales] That's not a tweak, that's a different design.
And the same review scored the display ninety-two per cent and called it the best laptop screen you can currently get.
So the best screen on sale is one some people can't look at.
Singapore prices start at three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine dollars for the fourteen-inch. Apple has said nothing, and there is no setting on a Mac to turn it off.
Is the number itself solid?

Honestly, disputed. One commenter went back to the measurement and could not reproduce it — he reads it as four hundred and eighty, possibly nine hundred and sixty. Go and wave your hand in front of one in a shop before you spend.
[wry] The consumer advice is: perform a small ritual in the Apple store.
The Atelier today is curtains. And the line is lovely.
Go on.
A curtain is two purchases pretending to be one. The cloth, and the workroom that makes it up. Almost all the money goes to the first and almost all the result to the second.
[curious] Which is why showrooms only ever talk about pattern.

And never about fullness. Which is the one thing you can check with a calculator — flat cloth against finished track. A three-metre track at two and a half times wants seven and a half metres of cloth.
And cheap made-to-measure?
Two or three widths in total. A pleat that collapses into a crease.
What about here, in the humidity?

The climate outranks the catalogue. Mean humidity is eighty-two per cent, and conservation guidance puts mould risk from sixty-five upward. Interlining is a napped wool blanket shut behind a closed curtain. Buy body as a heavier face cloth instead.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
Dry stone walling. A wall made of stone and nothing else.
No mortar, no cement, no glue. Nothing holds it together but weight, friction and the angle of its two faces. It cannot pull. It can only press.
[curious] So how does it stay up?

Counter-intuitively. Each stone goes in long end first, pointing into the wall rather than along the face, so the weight above pins it. The two faces lean inward as they rise, tipping each one's load toward the other. The cavity between is packed tight with small angular rubble. Because rounded gravel would act like ball bearings and shove the two faces apart.
[gasps] Oh, that's good. That's genuinely good.

And flat stones go clean across the full width, one about every metre, tying the two sides into one body. All of it is written down to the centimetre. The association publishes it: stones go in end in end out, and hearting must be thoroughly packed into the wall, and not just thrown in.
[amused] Somebody has been burned by thrown-in hearting.
Through stones spaced no more than one metre apart. The taper consistent along the full length. And copes must sit on their own base, rather than being propped up on pins.
How much of this stuff is there?
England and Wales, a hundred and five thousand eight hundred kilometres. Scotland another eighty-seven thousand one hundred. Ireland, on a single study, over four hundred thousand.
[drawn out] Four hundred thousand kilometres of wall.
And the only national condition data anybody quotes is fieldwork from nineteen ninety-four. Half of English walls in the three lowest categories. Thirteen per cent in good condition.
How big is the organised world of it?
Small. Britain's association had one thousand one hundred and thirty-nine members at the end of August last year, flat since twenty twenty-two and running a deficit.
And the kit? I'm imagining a van.

A hammer, a string, two steel pins and a wooden frame. That is the list, not a starter list. A waller of thirty years carries what a beginner carries, in better condition. One Vermont master is quoted as saying his equipment is a bucket with a hammer and a bit of string.
[laughs] So what does the money buy?

One thing. The ability to change the shape of a stone. A cheap hammer breaks stone where the stone wants to break. A hard-tipped one cuts where you want it to. Which makes the usable pile bigger and the day shorter. The association's own hammers run ninety-five pounds and a hundred and ten — and today four of the five patterns are out of stock. So are the pins and the lines.
[chuckles] The craft has a supply chain problem.
Only the thirty-five pound Pennine is available. And it will build a wall.
What's the grail end look like?

A complete American set at five hundred and thirty-nine dollars. A professional kit at one thousand nine hundred and twenty-nine. And a tracked power barrow at two and a half thousand pounds, if you have lost all discipline.
Is it a hobby, though? Honestly.

Honestly — no. It looks like a hobby from outside and behaves like a trade from inside. There is a four-rung exam: every timed test runs seven and a half hours, lunch excluded, not spread over multiple days, and all work must be the unaided work of the candidate.
[skeptical] And how many make the top grade?

Three Master Craftsmen qualified in the association's entire year. The top grade needs six years' professional experience, and an American body tells candidates that even talented wallers need five to ten years.
And from here? Can you do any of it in Singapore?
No. No body, no course, no register, no competition — not here, not Malaysia, Indonesia or Thailand. The British overseas register holds twenty-two names for the whole world.
[thoughtful] So the honest answer is you travel.
You travel. Japan's Ishizumi School teaches mortarless stacking by repairing hill-farm terraces. And a hundred pounds registers an overseas test site, so the examination can follow you home.
[warmly] I love that the exam will fly to you.

Culture, quickly. Johnny Depp's Scrooge opened at nineteen million dollars. Under the trade forecaster's floor. But the number underneath is the interesting one — fifty-four per cent with critics, ninety per cent with audiences.
[wry] Thirty-six points of daylight.
Which says it reached his existing audience and stopped. More than half the worldwide gross is from outside America.
And the week's steeper fall?
Godzilla Minus Zero, down eighty point eight per cent in its second weekend. On almost the same number of screens.
That's a distribution story, not a quality one.

Good Life. A small British maker opened orders this morning on a seven-hundred-and-fifty-pound calendar watch — date, moonphase, and a weekend indicator. Two years of work building the gears into a Chinese movement rather than stacking them on top. But the weekend indicator is set by hand.
[pause] Set by hand.
It tells you what you have already told it.
[laughs] It's a very expensive note to self.
Family desk. A weekly injection already licensed for adults cut body-mass index by about a fifth in twelve-to-seventeen-year-olds, over seventeen months, in a trial of a hundred and sixty.
And the caution?

Body-mass index is a surrogate. Nobody has shown that gap produces fewer adult heart attacks, and the comparator was a dummy injection rather than intensive lifestyle therapy. General guidance, not medical advice.
There's a second family story I liked more.

Fudan University followed four hundred and thirty-seven twelve-year-olds through three surveys. How closely either parent hovered predicted almost nothing about the child's internet use. What did predict it was how close the child felt to each parent. And what mattered most was the two parents being out of step with each other.
[warmly] Not how hard you watch. Whether you agree.

Fitness, and it is a tidy little result. Two rival ways of judging how close you are to failing a set agree to within a third of a repetition. Stop converting. But read it honestly — a p of zero point eight nine three is a failure to find a difference, not a demonstration of sameness. And one of the authors popularised one of the two scales.
[deadpan] The architects report that the building is standing.
And the long read. Bangladesh.
This is the certificate one.

The uprising that swept Sheikh Hasina out in August twenty twenty-four began as a protest about a certificate: a share of government jobs reserved for the descendants of men who fought a war in nineteen seventy-one. Twenty-seven months later, the state that revolution installed has issued thirteen thousand nine hundred and sixty-eight certificates of its own.
[pause] Of its own.

They are called July warriors, and the title is not honorific. It is a grade, and the grade is a price. Each class carries a lump sum, a monthly payment for life, and free treatment at any government hospital.
Who runs it?

The Ministry of Liberation War Affairs. The ministry of nineteen seventy-one. Graded by the same district officials who handle the older roll. And the education ministry put July families inside the same five per cent of school places reserved for freedom fighters.
[exhales] The same quota. With a second list feeding it.

Here is the number. The statute printed its own counts — four hundred and ninety-three in the top injury class. A ministry letter this month puts that class at nine hundred and ninety. It doubled. In a cohort injured on dates that cannot move.
And the older register? Does it tell us where this goes?
An Indian list surfaced in nineteen eighty-eight with sixty-nine thousand names. By February twenty twenty-four the ministry was funding two hundred and forty-one thousand.
[drawn out] From seventy thousand to two hundred and forty.

Amended at least seven times. Criteria changed eleven. Declared closed in January twenty twenty-four — six thousand pending applications and twenty-one thousand appeals extinguished at a stroke. And it did not stay closed. On the first of November this year the ministry ordered every verification committee reconstituted, to begin again. Nine days later it told districts to invite new July applications.
Two registers, one ministry, one fortnight.

And in April an elected Parliament replaced the emergency ordinance with an Act — twenty-five sections for twenty-five, interim government becomes government. And section eleven still certifies the old figures. Fourteen months after the ministry had moved past them.
[thoughtful] The legislature didn't revise the count. It engraved it.

Run the counter-case, because it is serious. The government recognises eight hundred and forty-two dead; the United Nations human rights office estimated as many as one thousand four hundred. Nine hundred and thirty-one applications are stuck at district level, and the foundation needs four hundred crore taka and has received a hundred and nineteen.
So it might be a backlog reaching people who were always entitled.
It might. The reply is that underpayment and inflation are the same disease. A register that cannot say how many died, yet has doubled its most expensive class, is not clearing a backlog.
[pause] It is losing the ability to tell a claim from a fact.
A list is the only thanks a state knows how to give. And the only way a list can honour more people is to get longer.
[warmly] That's the line of the issue.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
